name: Lawunuia
confidence_why: Capell 1971 only suggested from his 1963 survey wordlists that stress might be phonemic in Nagarige (ˈvisuna 'his nose' vs viˈsuna 'her breast') while himself recording the Amun forms with a vowel-length difference, Lincoln 1975, working first-hand in all four Banoni-Piva varieties, found no word distinguished by stress or pitch and treats vowel length as the contrast, and neither says where stress falls, so nothing about Lawunuia stress placement is known.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Capell tentatively suggests that stress is contrastive (lexical) in Nagarige (= Piva/Lawunuia) on the strength of one near-minimal pair from his 1963 survey vocabulary (ˈvisuna 'his nose' vs viˈsuna 'her breast'), but immediately notes that in the Amun dialect of the same language the pair differs segmentally (vi-ˈisuna vs viˈsuuna, i.e. an extra vowel / vowel length), and concludes only that the languages need further study. No placement rule is given. (For the sister language Banoni, Lynch & Ross 2002:441 give penultimate stress on vowel-final words, final on consonant-final words, with phonemic vowel length, which would make Capell's pair a length contrast rather than a stress contrast; nothing equivalent has been published for Piva itself.)
new_statements.exceptions: The Amun dialect forms (vi-ˈisuna / viˈsuuna) are presented by Capell himself as counter-evidence to a stress analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (possessed nouns with 3sg suffix -na) from a survey wordlist; word level. Capell treats Nagarige and Amun as dialects of 'Banoni'; both are Lawunuia (lawu1237) varieties in current classification.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell (1971) calls the variety 'Nagarige' (with a northern enclave dialect 'Amun') and treats both as dialects of Banoni; Glottolog/OLAC list Nagarige, Naghareghe, Piva and Amun as names of Lawunuia (lawu1237, ISO tgi), distinct from Banoni proper (bano1247, ISO bcm). The only explicit stress RULE in print (penultimate on V-final words, final on C-final words; Lynch & Ross 2002:441) is for Banoni (bano1247), not Lawunuia, and should not be transferred without a Piva-specific source.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (and pitch) is audible in all four west-coast Bougainville varieties Lincoln surveyed (Amun, Piva, Torokina, Mabes) but was never found to distinguish two words, i.e. word stress is non-contrastive; no placement rule is given. The contrast Capell attributed to stress is carried by vowel length in Lincoln's data: p. 63 'Vowels may occur distinctively lengthened or short', [tʃi:] 'garamut' vs [tʃi] 'can, be able'. The orthography (sec. 4-5) writes long vowels by doubling the letter and does not mark stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; Lincoln flags Piva's 'particularly lively use of pitch range' as needing further investigation, and p. 57 warns the analysis is tentative
new_statements.identity_note: Lincoln 1975 is primarily a description of the Mabes variety of Banoni proper (Tsunari, ISO bcm, Glottolog bann1247) with notes on Torokina, Piva and Amun; he groups Amun + Piva as the 'Piva language' ([raβunuia] / [raŋunuia] / [naɣareɣe]), which is Lawunuia (lawu1237, alt. names Nagarige/Piva), and Torokina + Mabes as the 'Banoni language' ([tsunari]). The stress statement is made for 'all varieties' and so applies to Lawunuia (Amun and Piva) as well as Banoni; the vowel-length examples are Mabes forms. The Glottolog record for this work (ref 8010) codes it as Bannoni [bcm].

readall_conflicts: Capell 1971 (CTL 8, pp. 281-282; the catalog's existing statement, already read as 'unclear or contradictory') suggests from survey wordlists that stress 'can be phonemic' in Nagarige (ˈvisuna 'his nose' vs viˈsuna 'her breast') but immediately notes that the Amun dialect shows the same pair as a vowel-length difference (vi-ˈisuna vs viˈsuuna). Lincoln 1975, p. 64, from first-hand work on all four varieties, states that stress and pitch were nowhere found to distinguish two words and that vowel length is distinctive (p. 63). So the sources disagree on whether Lawunuia has contrastive word stress: Capell tentatively yes (Nagarige), Lincoln no (all varieties, length instead). Neither source gives a placement rule. Lincoln's own caveat (p. 57: tentative analysis) and his remark that Piva's pitch range 'should be investigated further' leave the prosody of Piva open. The Banoni Mabes OPD (2006, ed. P. Lincoln; Banoni proper, not Lawunuia; downloaded for context) likewise lists only phonemic vowel length under 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' and says nothing about stress.
